Hero Photography · Fiji
South Pacific

The Warm Heart
of the Pacific.

Fiji is the destination that delivers what the South Pacific brand actually promises — a genuine welcome that isn't manufactured for tourism, private island resorts at a scale and intimacy the Caribbean cannot match, and soft coral diving that serious divers rank among the finest in the world. The work of planning Fiji is choosing the right island chain — Mamanuca, Yasawa, or the more remote Lau Group — and matching the property to the trip.

The Country

Private Islands at a Scale
Most Categories Can't Match.

Fiji's distinctive offer in the South Pacific is the private-island resort category — a genuinely uninhabited island, a lodge of 12 to 20 rooms maximum, a reef wrapping the property, and a staff ratio that makes a Botswana safari camp look crowded. The format exists in scattered form across the Pacific and the Indian Ocean, but Fiji has the highest density of this kind of property in the world. The Mamanuca and Yasawa chains contain more than a dozen such resorts, ranging from honeymoon-focused intimate properties (adults-only, 14 villas) to family-accessible reef-and-snorkel destinations.

The Bligh Waters between Fiji's two main islands (Viti Levu and Vanua Levu) are widely considered by serious divers to contain the finest soft coral diving on earth — the colors of the soft coral species are genuinely unlike anything in the Caribbean or Mediterranean, and the visibility in the channels is consistently 30+ meters. The Rainbow Reef off Taveuni and the Great White Wall (a sheer vertical face of densely packed white soft coral) are the destination dives. Travelers who have done Cozumel and the Red Sea consistently describe Fiji's soft coral as a different category of underwater experience.

Fiji's welcome is the third element that distinguishes it. The Bula greeting is not a tourism affectation — it's a genuine cultural expression that runs through every interaction in the country, from the resort staff to the village kava ceremony to the airport baggage handler. The villages around the resort properties remain functioning communities, and the lodges that organize a village visit (with the appropriate sevusevu of yaqona/kava as a gift to the village chief) deliver one of the most authentic cultural exchanges available anywhere in the South Pacific.

Where We Send Clients

Six Versions of Fiji Worth Planning Around

Fiji has 332 islands; the question is never which island, it's which version of Fiji you're after. Each of these six covers a different format, a different vibe, and a different reason to make the long Pacific flight.

Destination Photography · Yasawa Islands
Western Fiji
Yasawa Islands
The most remote of the easily accessible island chains — a string of 20 volcanic islands stretching 80 km northwest from Viti Levu. Access by seaplane (45 minutes from Nadi) or by Yasawa Flyer catamaran (4–5 hours, the working ferry that also delivers supplies to the island villages). The private island resorts here run small (12–24 rooms typical) and the snorkeling off the reefs at properties like Yasawa Island Resort and Turtle Island delivers manta ray encounters at Drawaqa during the May–October season. The village of Nacula is the cultural visit warranting the sevusevu kava gift; the village chief still receives travelers in the traditional way.
Private Islands Manta Rays Seaplane Access May–October

Destination Photography · Mamanuca Islands
Western Fiji
Mamanuca Islands
The closer of the two western chains — 20 minutes by boat from Denarau or 10 minutes by seaplane from Nadi. The Mamanucas contain the largest concentration of resort properties in Fiji, ranging from the family-focused (Castaway Island, Malolo) to the adults-only honeymoon (Tokoriki, Tadrai). The reef snorkeling immediately off the resorts is consistently excellent. Day trips to Cloud 9 (the floating bar over a coral atoll) for travelers who want the social scene. The trade-off vs. the Yasawas: less remote feel, but significantly easier access and more property variety.
Resort Density Family Options Easy Access Cloud 9
Explore →
Destination Photography · Vanua Levu & Taveuni
Northern Fiji
Vanua Levu & Taveuni
The northern islands and the diving capital of Fiji. The Rainbow Reef between Vanua Levu and Taveuni produces the famous Great White Wall dive — a sheer vertical face of densely packed white soft coral that drops from 15m to 60m, with current dives along the wall encountering grey reef sharks, hammerheads (seasonally), and the soft coral colors that give the channel its name. The Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort on Savusavu is the destination property for serious divers. Taveuni itself — the Garden Island — has the 180th meridian running through it (you can stand with one foot in today and one in tomorrow) and a hiking culture distinct from the rest of Fiji.
Great White Wall Soft Coral Diving Cousteau Resort Taveuni
Explore →
Destination Photography · Lau Group
Eastern Fiji
Lau Group
The most remote inhabited Fijian archipelago — a chain of 60 islands in the eastern part of the country, accessible primarily by chartered yacht or by the occasional liveaboard expedition. The Lau Group has been the most strictly preserved cultural and natural area of Fiji, with traditional village life still operating largely as it did before European contact. Vatuvara Private Islands is the only luxury resort property in the chain (1 villa, fly-in access, deeply private). For travelers who have done Bali and Fiji and want a South Pacific that has not changed in fifty years, the Lau Group is the answer.
Most Remote Traditional Culture Charter Yacht Vatuvara
Explore →
Destination Photography · Coral Coast
Southern Viti Levu
Coral Coast & Pacific Harbour
The mainland Viti Levu's southern coast, where the larger resort properties (Outrigger, InterContinental, Naviti) are situated within reach of land-based activities. Best for travelers who want a Fiji that combines beach time with rainforest day trips, Sigatoka River whitewater, the Garden of the Sleeping Giant orchid collection, and a base of operations for sport-fishing. Pacific Harbour is the bull and tiger shark diving capital of Fiji — Beqa Lagoon has shark dives that consistently bring bull sharks and tiger sharks into close proximity with divers, a controlled commercial dive operation that has run for decades.
Mainland Resorts Bull Shark Diving Beqa Lagoon Land-based Activities
Explore →
Destination Photography · Kadavu
Southern Fiji
Kadavu & the Great Astrolabe Reef
Fiji's fourth-largest island and the gateway to the Great Astrolabe Reef — the world's fourth-longest barrier reef, encircling the island and producing diving conditions that compete with the Rainbow Reef in coral diversity and the Bligh Waters in current dives. The lodges here are intimate (Matava is widely considered Fiji's most genuine eco-resort), the island has very little tourism infrastructure outside of the resort properties, and the village visits feel less rehearsed than on the more developed islands. For a Fiji trip that emphasizes diving and a more authentic island feel over resort luxury.

Featured Itineraries

Trips We Plan Often

Fiji itineraries built around the right private island, the right access (seaplane vs catamaran vs ferry), and the right combination of beach, diving, and village culture for the trip you actually want.

Itinerary Photography
Yasawa Island Resort
May – October · 8–10 Days
Yasawa Islands Private Resort
Fly into Nadi, overnight at a Denarau resort to recover from the international flight. Seaplane to a small Yasawa private-island resort (12–20 rooms) for 7 nights — reef snorkeling immediately off the property, manta ray encounter at Drawaqa Passage in season (May–October, when the plankton bloom attracts the rays), a village visit with the kava sevusevu, a beach picnic at an uninhabited motu. Return by seaplane to Nadi for one final night before the international flight home. The format that delivers the Fiji that the marketing photographs promise.
Fiji8–10 Days
Itinerary Photography
Fiji Diving Circuit
April – October · 10–12 Days
Fiji Diving: Vanua Levu & the Great White Wall
For divers. Fly into Nadi, connecting flight to Savusavu on Vanua Levu, 7 nights at the Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort with daily diving on the Rainbow Reef, the Great White Wall, and the Namena Marine Reserve. Connect to Taveuni for a 3-day extension at one of the island's dive lodges with focused current dives along the Rainbow Reef from a closer base. Return through Nadi for a beach decompression night. The diving credentials needed: Open Water minimum, Advanced strongly recommended, Nitrox helpful for the deeper Great White Wall dives.
Fiji10–12 Days
Itinerary Photography
Fiji Family Resort
Year-Round · 8–10 Days
Fiji Family: Mamanucas
For families with children. Fly into Nadi, transfer by boat (45 minutes) to a Mamanuca family-resort property (Castaway, Malolo, or Likuliku) for 7 nights. Resort programs for children of all ages (the Bula Club for toddlers; supervised activities for teens), excellent immediate-reef snorkeling, swimming pools, kayaks and paddleboards. Optional day trip to Cloud 9 or to a nearby uninhabited motu for the castaway lunch experience. Final night at the InterContinental on Denarau for a smoother airport morning. Fiji is one of the strongest family destinations in the South Pacific when paired with the right family-specific resort.
Fiji8–10 Days
Itinerary Photography
Lau Group Charter
May – October · 10–14 Days
Lau Group: Private Charter
For travelers who have done Fiji and want the deepest experience available. Private yacht charter (8–12 guests, full crew) from Savusavu departing east into the Lau Group for 7–10 days. Anchor at uninhabited islands, dive virgin reefs with no prior commercial visitation, attend village welcome ceremonies in villages that receive perhaps a dozen visitors per year. Return to Savusavu for connection back to Nadi. Alternative: Vatuvara Private Islands resort in the northern Lau Group as a fixed lodge option (1 villa total, exclusive use, fly-in by chartered Twin Otter).

Why Plan With Us

What We Add to Fiji Planning

Fiji is the destination where the private-island resort selection, the access method (seaplane vs catamaran), and the diving operator quality combine to produce a trip that either delivers the South Pacific archetype or feels like a generic beach holiday.

⬡
Private Island Resort Selection
Fiji has more private-island resorts than any other destination in the world — and the range across them is wide. Some are genuinely intimate (12 rooms, no other guests outside of the dining hall), some are larger and busier (60+ rooms, an active social scene). Some are adults-only and honeymoon-focused; some are family-accessible with kids' programs and shallow snorkel access. Some have outstanding reef immediately off the dock; some require a 20-minute boat ride to reach the good snorkeling. These differences are not apparent in marketing materials; they require firsthand knowledge.
⬡
Access Logistics
Fiji's outer islands are accessed by seaplane (10–45 minutes, dramatic arrival, expensive), by helicopter (10–30 minutes, similar cost), by Yasawa Flyer catamaran (4–5 hours, scenic and cheaper, with stops at multiple islands en route), or by speedboat transfer (45–90 minutes, mid-range). The right access method depends on the destination resort, the time of arrival in Nadi (afternoon arrivals usually mean a Denarau overnight, since seaplane operations don't run at dusk), and the comfort with overwater transport. We sequence the access to minimize wasted time.
⬡
Soft Coral Diving Operator Quality
The Bligh Waters and the Rainbow Reef have a reputation among serious divers that the right operator can deliver and the wrong operator can completely miss. The current dives on the Great White Wall require precise timing against the tides — a 30-minute window difference produces a different experience. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort's dive operation and a small number of independent operators in Savusavu and Taveuni have the local current expertise; the larger general-purpose operations frequently do not.
⬡
Village & Cultural Programming
The village visit (with the appropriate sevusevu of yaqona/kava as a gift to the village chief) is one of the most genuine cultural exchanges available in the South Pacific, but it has to be arranged through a property that has a real relationship with the local village rather than a commercial arrangement. The properties we recommend have multi-generational relationships with the surrounding villages, and the visit format is genuine cultural exchange rather than performance for visitors. We make sure clients understand the appropriate protocols.
When to Go

Fiji by Season

Dry Season
May – October
The reliable Fiji window — cooler air (mid-70s to low 80s), lower humidity, reduced rainfall, and the most stable diving conditions. The trade winds keep the temperatures comfortable. May, June, and September are the sweet spot for crowd avoidance and rate access. July and August are the European/Australian peak. Manta ray season at Drawaqa Passage in the Yasawas runs roughly May through October. Visibility on the Bligh Waters and the Rainbow Reef is at its peak. The Fijian winter is genuinely temperate rather than hot, which makes the long days outside resort-comfortable.
Best Overall Window
Shoulder Months
November & April
The shoulder months between the dry and wet seasons — warm but not yet in the cyclone window, with some rainfall increase but largely good weather. November is one of our preferred booking windows: trades remain consistent, rates drop from the July–August peak, and the manta ray season is winding down (which makes the latest-season encounters often the most concentrated). April is similarly attractive — recovering from the wet season, with the diving visibility returning to peak conditions and significantly lower rates at most resorts.
Wet Season
December – March
Fiji's wet season — warmer (mid-80s), higher humidity, more frequent and intense rainfall, and the official cyclone window (which doesn't typically affect tourist islands but occasionally disrupts travel logistics). The water temperature remains warm, the diving is still possible (though visibility drops on the open reef sites), and rates at most resorts drop meaningfully. Christmas through early January is the Australian/New Zealand school holiday peak — busy and pricier than the rest of the wet season. February is the rainiest month and the one most travelers should avoid.

A Note from Mark

On Fiji's Distinctive Format

Mark Sole
Founder & Travel Director · Hit Your Mark Travel

"Fiji's private-island resort format is the South Pacific at its most distinctive — a 12-room lodge on an island whose only other inhabitants are the staff and the village it sits next to, with a reef wrapping the property and a guide who has worked these waters for fifteen years. The format exists in scattered form elsewhere — Mnemba off Zanzibar, the more remote Maldives — but Fiji has the highest density of these kinds of properties in the world. The trip we sell isn't the Bula greeting at the airport. It's the moment three days in when the staff knows your name and the kava ceremony in the village starts because you specifically have arrived. That requires the right property and the right village relationship. We know which combinations deliver."

Common Questions

Fiji — FAQ

Questions we hear most when planning Fiji — from Mamanuca vs Yasawa to seaplane access, diving certification, and how to choose the right private island resort.

Mamanuca versus Yasawa — which chain should I choose?+
Mamanuca for easier access (10–45 minutes from Nadi), more resort variety, more family-focused options, and slightly busier social scenes. Yasawa for the more remote feel, smaller and more intimate private-island resorts, the manta ray season (May–October at Drawaqa Passage), and less developed surrounding villages. For a first Fiji trip with the standard 7–10 day length, either chain delivers a strong experience; the Yasawas typically produce the more memorable single trip if the schedule accommodates the seaplane access.
Is Fiji good for families with children?+
Yes — one of the strongest family destinations in the South Pacific when matched to the right property. The Mamanuca family-resort properties (Castaway, Malolo, Likuliku) have well-staffed kids' programs across age groups, excellent immediate-reef snorkeling, and a Fijian welcome culture that treats children warmly and inclusively. The Yasawas have fewer family options but excellent properties for older children and teens. The honeymoon-focused adults-only properties (Tokoriki, Tadrai, Vatuvara) are not family destinations.
What is the diving certification requirement for the Great White Wall?+
Open Water minimum, Advanced Open Water strongly recommended (the wall drops from 15m to 60m, with most of the soft coral concentration below 18m). Nitrox certification is helpful for longer dive times at depth. The dive operators at Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort and the Taveuni dive operations require evidence of Advanced certification for the deeper sections of the wall. For the inside-lagoon sites, Open Water with limited prior experience is sufficient. Less-experienced divers can still see significant soft coral at shallower depths on alternative reef sites.
When is the best time to visit Fiji?+
May through October is the dry season and the right answer for almost every traveler. May, June, and September are the sweet spot — same weather as July–August, with lower crowds and better rates. The manta ray season at Drawaqa Passage in the Yasawas runs roughly May through October, with August–September often producing the most concentrated encounters. November and April are excellent shoulder months. December through March is the wet season and the cyclone window — significantly cheaper but with weather variability and occasional disruption to logistics.
How does Fiji compare to French Polynesia?+
Fiji has more genuine cultural depth (the Fijian village culture is more accessible to visitors than the equivalent in French Polynesia), better diving (the soft coral of the Bligh Waters is genuinely a different category from anything in French Polynesia), more private-island resort variety, and notably lower price points across most resort categories. French Polynesia has the iconic Bora Bora lagoon view, more architecturally elaborate overwater villas at the top end, and a more romantic honeymoon archetype. For divers and cultural travelers, Fiji is the stronger answer; for honeymooners specifically looking for the Bora Bora photograph, French Polynesia.
Is the Fiji welcome a tourism affectation or genuine?+
Genuine, in our experience consistently. The Bula greeting runs through every Fijian interaction — at airports, at fuel stations, at the resort, in the village. Fijian hospitality culture is structured around the principle that the guest is the most important person in the room, and the cultural overlay holds up across the country regardless of tourism economics. This is one of the consistent factors that produces the high client return-rate on Fiji trips — travelers describe being changed by the warmth of the welcome in a way that doesn't match the South Pacific resort archetype they expected.
What is the kava (yaqona) ceremony?+
A traditional Fijian welcome ceremony that involves the preparation and sharing of kava, a non-alcoholic drink made from the powdered root of the kava plant. The drink produces a mild numbing sensation in the mouth and a relaxed mental state. The ceremony is structured around the chief and senior village members and is the traditional way to enter a village as a visitor. Travelers participate by bringing a bundle of kava root (yaqona) as a sevusevu gift, which the resort or guide will provide. The ceremony is one of the most genuine cultural exchanges available in the South Pacific when arranged through a property with a real village relationship.
Do I need to worry about the cyclone season?+
The official South Pacific cyclone season runs November through April, with the peak risk between January and March. Cyclones that affect Fiji's tourist regions occur on average every few years; most years pass without significant disruption to travel. The risk affects the wet-season trip planning more as a weather-variability question than as a cyclone-specific concern. Travel insurance that covers weather disruption is appropriate for wet-season Fiji trips. We don't recommend Fiji in February specifically (peak risk + heaviest rains); November, March, and April carry low risk despite being shoulder months.
